Surely, you are wrong in having impri- soned such a powerful friend and ally. If, notwith- standing th^ common cause, the Government answer to the Congress demand is hasty repression they will not wonder if I draw the inference that it was not so much the Allied cause tibat weighed with the British Government as the unexpressal determina- tion to cling to the possession of India as an indis- pensable part of the imperial policy. The determina- tion led to the rejection of the Congress demand and precipitated repression. The present mutual slaughter on a scale never before known to history is suffocat- ing enough. But the slaughter of truth accompany- ing the butchery and enforced by the falsity of which the resolution is reeking adds strength to the Congress position. It causes me deep pain to have to send you this long letter. But however much I dislike your action, I remain the same friend you have known me. I would still plead for reoonsideraticm of the Government of India’s whole policy- Do not dis- r^ard Cbe pleading of one who daims to be a sincere friend of  the  British people. Heaven guide you. I am. Yours sincerely, M. K. GANDHI.
